clue.text: Our pirate changes into appropriate riding kit

indicators.note: Something that changes into something else does not come out in the order it went in, so the letters beside it are to be rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
whatever is appropriate for a job is fit for it, and those three letters join the shuffle

explanation.surface: A pirate of ours getting changed into the proper gear for a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective in front of 'kit' and is really three more letters of fodder. Nine letters plus those three make twelve, so nothing is being added or dropped along the way.
explanation.definitionFit: The puncture repair outfit of patches and glue is the kit a cyclist carries when out riding, not the jodhpurs 'riding' first suggests.

clue.text: Spoil sport at home

blocks.note: RU is rugby union, the shorthand on a British fixture list
somebody at home is in when you call round

explanation.surface: A killjoy sitting about the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoil sport' wants to be read as one word, the killjoy, and the split falls after the first word, which is a verb here. Sport in a grid is usually one of the abbreviations off a fixture list.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin something is to wreck it beyond use, the strongest sense of spoil — spoil a view, ruin a view.

clue.text: Secret serviceman

blocks.note: kept from other people, not for general eyes — a confidential conversation, an undisclosed income
the lowest rank in the army, the soldier with no stripe on the sleeve

explanation.surface: A member of the secret service.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, and no join at all: 'Secret serviceman' reads as one job and has to be pulled apart. The army rank runs from private up through corporal and sergeant.
explanation.definitionFit: A private matter is one kept secret, and a private is the lowest rank of soldier — the adjective and the noun spelt the same way.

clue.text: Mental picture I'm getting before time

indicators.note: Before puts what precedes it in front, so the contraction is written ahead of the second piece rather than after it.

blocks.note: the clue's own contraction, its two letters lifted straight off the page
an age is a long stretch of time — the Bronze Age, waited an age

explanation.surface: A vision arriving in somebody's head ahead of schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm getting' reads as a sentence about the solver, and the two letters of the contraction are taken exactly as written. Time measured long rather than short is what gives the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is the picture held in the mind's eye as much as one on paper, which is what a mental picture is.

clue.text: Aim to lodge a protest

blocks.note: the end somebody has in view, the purpose of the whole business
to stand up and say you are against it, at a planning meeting or in court

explanation.surface: Somebody setting out to make a formal complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the clue is one person's intention to complain, and the two halves have to be split instead. The noun is stressed on its first syllable and the verb on its second.
explanation.definitionFit: An object is what you aim at or aim to do; to object is to protest — noun and verb, told apart in speech by which syllable is stressed.

clue.text: Wavy lines in note made to stretch

indicators.note: A wavy line will not run straight, and letters that will not run straight are to be rearranged.
In puts the letters just shuffled inside the word that follows, splitting it open rather than standing beside it.

blocks.note: TE is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale: do re mi fa so la te
the five letters of the lines, rearranged

explanation.surface: Squiggles drawn on a memo about stretching.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters of note have to come apart to let five more sit between them, which is why the shorter piece is the one that opens up. 'Wavy lines' looks like a picture and is fodder plus its instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A tensile material takes a pull without snapping — tensile strength is what a rope is sold on — so it is made for stretching.

clue.text: Drive little devil to join the Spanish

blocks.note: an imp is a small mischievous demon, the grid's standing naughty child
the Spanish word for 'the' is el

explanation.surface: Pushing a mischievous child into signing up with the Spaniards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' is the verb for urging somebody on rather than anything to do with a car, and it stands alone at the front. Grids ask for foreign articles constantly: Spanish gives EL or LA, French LE or LA.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel someone is to push or urge them into acting, which is drive used as a verb — what drives you and what impels you are one force.

clue.text: Not unhappy with coloured whiskey bottled

indicators.note: Bottled means shut inside a container.

blocks.note: cloth that has been coloured has been dyed
rye is the grain an American whiskey is distilled from, and the name of the drink itself

explanation.surface: A drinker content enough now the tinted whiskey is in the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whiskey' with the E is the Irish and American spelling, and the grain in it is what the clue wants. 'Bottled' works both ways at once: it keeps the surface on drink and says one word goes inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Not unhappy is the setter's roundabout way of saying not in tears: eyes that are dry are eyes that have not been crying.

clue.text: With tip of shinbone missing, last character stuck in Balearic island

indicators.note: The tip of a word is the letter it starts with, the point you come to first.
Missing says that letter is not in the answer — take it off before anything else happens.
Stuck in puts the letter named right inside what is left, not on either end of it.

blocks.note: the tibia is the shinbone, the big bone between knee and ankle
the opening letter of the bone's name, and the clue takes it away
the alphabet's final letter, wedged in before what is now the last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip of' asks for a first letter, so the shinbone loses its T before anything else is done. The character stuck in is the last of the alphabet — nothing in the clue spells it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is one of the Balearics, the Spanish islands off Valencia, and the one known for its clubs.

clue.text: First of the month for each berry

blocks.note: a date written short: JUN for June with the Roman numeral I for the first day
per means for each — sixty miles per hour

explanation.surface: A calendar note: the first of the month, one for every berry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of' looks like an instruction to take an opening letter, which would give T from 'the month'. It is a date instead, a month's abbreviation with the Roman numeral for one behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The juniper's blue-black cones are the berries that flavour gin, so the shrub's name does duty for its fruit.

clue.text: Bird to dance at Irish party, say

indicators.note: Say asks for the noise the words in front of it make rather than the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: to caper is to skip and frolic about
a ceilidh is a Gaelic evening of dancing and fiddle music, and its Gaelic spelling is nothing like the noise it makes

explanation.surface: A bird invited to dance at an Irish get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: The capercaillie is the giant grouse of the Scottish pine forests, the male of which fans its tail like a turkey. A ceilidh said aloud is 'kay-lee', which is where the second half of the spelling comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The capercaillie is the largest European grouse, a woodland game bird, so 'Bird' names it by its class.

clue.text: Member of conspiracy when poor Hermes catches cold

indicators.note: Something in poor condition has fallen apart, and letters that have fallen apart can go back together in any order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder: the Greek messenger god's name, six letters
C is the letter on the cold tap, a standing abbreviation

explanation.surface: A shabby-looking Hermes going down with a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' reads as pity for the god rather than as a state his letters are in. The cold hands over a single letter, which is why seven come out of a six-letter name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone hatching a secret plan is a schemer, and the people inside a conspiracy are exactly the ones doing the hatching.

clue.text: Emperor races off round front of amphitheatre

indicators.note: Something that has gone off has come apart, so the word beside it is to be taken to pieces and reassembled.
Going round a thing takes it in, so the single letter ends up among the letters being rearranged rather than outside them.
The front of a word is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
the letter at the front of the word

explanation.surface: An emperor sprinting away round the front of the arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Races off' reads as the emperor bolting and is the fodder with its own shuffle instruction attached. Five letters plus the amphitheatre's first make the six the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar was the family name that became the Roman title for the man in charge, and it carried on into Kaiser and Tsar.

clue.text: A laboratory turns up single sea creature

indicators.note: A down answer is written from the top, so what turns up is read from the bottom instead — the letters come out the other way round.

blocks.note: the clue's first word, taken as it stands
a laboratory is a lab, and those three letters are then read the other way
a single of anything is one of them

explanation.surface: A laboratory coming up with one solitary sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns up' does two jobs: in the surface the lab produces something, and in the grid the shortened laboratory is read from the bottom. Abalone shells are the iridescent ones sold as mother-of-pearl.
explanation.definitionFit: The abalone is an edible sea snail that clings to rocks in an ear-shaped shell, so 'sea creature' is the broad class it belongs to.

clue.text: Weak complaint returned by the French

indicators.note: Returned sends the letters back the way they came, so across the grid they read from right to left.

blocks.note: a beef is a grumble or complaint, and here it is written back to front
the French word for 'the' is le

explanation.surface: A grumble sent back to us by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: The word that gets turned round is never printed: 'complaint' has to become the slang beef first, and only then has 'returned' got something to work on. The French for 'the' is LE or LA, depending on gender.
explanation.definitionFit: Something feeble lacks strength — a feeble grip, a feeble excuse — which is the everyday meaning of weak.

clue.text: Cry of approval about commercial show of courage

indicators.note: About means around, so the letters named next are taken inside the word in front of them.

blocks.note: the shout from the stalls when a singer has done well
a commercial on television is an ad

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic shout about an advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: Bravado is courage put on for show rather than felt, so the definition flatters it. 'About' is the mildest of container words and reads easily as the subject of the shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is daring put on for display, so the phrase catches the show while leaving out the courage behind it.

clue.text: Good person placing a bet first, optimally

indicators.note: Placing letters is setting them down where you choose, a loose way of saying they need not keep the order they arrived in.
First says which of the two pieces leads.

blocks.note: the two words taken as they stand, four letters of fodder
a good person is a saint, and a saint in front of a name shortens to two letters

explanation.surface: A decent sort getting a wager in early.
explanation.walkthrough: A good person is the saint of the calendar, and the wager beside it hands over four more letters. The comma is the only sign that the fodder has stopped and the definition has begun.
explanation.definitionFit: At best means taking the most favourable view — at best it will hold till Friday — which is doing something optimally.

clue.text: One's in the kitchen, no longer supporter of farm vehicle?

definitions.note: The definition is a whole sentence with 'one' standing in for the answer — the thing you would point at in a kitchen — rather than a noun phrase.

blocks.note: what is no longer the case takes the prefix ex- — an ex-wife, an ex-serviceman
the machine that pulls a plough up and down a field
a supporter of a team or a singer is a fan

explanation.surface: Someone in the kitchen who has gone off tractors.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that an ex-tractor fan is a lapsed enthusiast, and the same letters respace into a kitchen appliance. 'Supporter of farm vehicle' has to be read as the tractor's fan, which puts the vehicle first.
explanation.definitionFit: An extractor fan is the grille over a hob that pulls steam and cooking smells out of the room, so the one in the kitchen is exactly that.

clue.text: Pace around a set of cards

indicators.note: Around means encircling, so the letter named next is taken inside the word before it.

blocks.note: a trot is a horse's pace, between a walk and a canter
the clue's own indefinite article, taken as a single letter

explanation.surface: Pacing up and down beside a spread of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pace' is the horse's gait rather than walking the floor, and what it swallows is the ordinary article of the clue. Tarot packs carry twenty-two picture cards on top of the four suits.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarot is the old pack used for fortune-telling, with the Fool, the Hanged Man and the rest, so it is a set of cards rather than a game.

clue.text: Studies marsh grasses, we hear

indicators.note: We hear asks for the sound of the words in front of it, not the letters they are written with.

blocks.note: the tall grasses standing in shallow water are reeds, and said aloud they are spelt another way

explanation.surface: Overhearing somebody on the subject of the grasses in a marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: Reeds and the word wanted are an exact pair of homophones in British English, differing only on the page. 'Studies' is the verb: to read history at university is to study it.
explanation.definitionFit: To read a subject at university is to study it, and both words carry the same third-person -s.

clue.text: Some authoritarian deity

indicators.note: Some asks for a part of the word beside it rather than all of it, and that part is already spelt out there in order.

blocks.note: four letters running unbroken from the third letter of the word

explanation.surface: A god with a taste for absolute rule.
explanation.walkthrough: A concealment inside one long word is the hardest kind to spot, because the eye reads a long word as a single shape. Thor is the Norse thunder god, the one with the hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thor is the hammer-wielding Norse god of thunder, so 'deity' names him by his class rather than by name.

clue.text: Noble order is a feature

blocks.note: an earl is the British peer ranking between a marquess and a viscount
the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, the honour handed out at the Palace

explanation.surface: A rank of nobility counted as a distinguishing mark.
explanation.walkthrough: The join falls inside a word: the peer's four letters run straight into the honour's three, so 'Noble order' reads as one phrase about the aristocracy. The feature wanted is one of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: The ear lobe is the soft flap hanging at the bottom of the ear, one of the features a face is described by.

clue.text: Cause embarrassment at a party

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken as a letter
slang for a big noisy party, the sort you throw

explanation.surface: Making somebody blush at a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a party' reads as where the blushing happens and is really the letters: the clue's article, then the slang for a party. Nothing is hidden, turned or shuffled — the pieces are set down in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash someone is to knock their confidence and leave them embarrassed; the word survives mostly in its opposite, unabashed.

clue.text: Note adder's tooth removed on the way out?

indicators.note: Something removed has been taken out of its place, and letters out of their places are to be put back in another order.

blocks.note: A is the musical note an orchestra tunes to
eleven letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing

explanation.surface: A memo that the adder had a fang taken out on its way off the premises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is the musical A rather than an instruction to observe, and 'removed' is the shuffle, not a deletion — nothing leaves the fodder. The answer's own apostrophe comes free with the adder's.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody at death's door is not expected to live, which is what 'on the way out' means of a person rather than of a fashion.
